extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, IPR parties, patent examiners, and judges
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary criteria used in inter partes review to evaluate whether patent claims are anticipated under 35 U.S.C. § 102 or obvious under 35 U.S.C. § 103, including how to treat combinations of prior art, inherency, motivation to combine, and proof of public accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham obviousness factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of obviousness is resolved on the basis of underlying factual determinations including: (1) the scope and content of the prior art; (2) any differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art; (3) the level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) objective evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Graham v. John Deere. These four factual inquiries frame the obviousness inquiry and guide whether a claimed invention would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation/suggestion to combine references
rubrics_metrics.description: When all elements of a claim are found in various pieces of prior art, the factfinder must consider whether a person of ordinary skill in the art would be motivated to combine those references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A suggested motivation or teaching to combine references must exist; courts look for some suggestion, teaching, or motivation in the prior art (or the knowledge of a skilled artisan) to combine the references. Citations: Dome Patent L.P. v. Lee; WMS Gaming; Concrete Pipe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation of success when combining
rubrics_metrics.description: When combining references, it must be shown that a person of ordinary skill would have had a reasonable expectation of success in making the combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expectation of success must be founded in the prior art (not the applicant's disclosure) and requires more than mere speculation—there must be a reasonable likelihood the combination would work. See In re Magnum Oil Tools; In re Dow Chemical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestion and expectation must be based in prior art (not applicant disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both the suggestion (or motivation) to combine references and the expectation of success must be founded in the prior art, not in the applicant’s disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments that rely on the patent owner's own disclosure to supply the motivation or expectation are improper. See In re Dow Chemical; In re Magnum Oil Tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR ‘obvious to try’ / predictable solutions principle
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention may be found obvious if trying a course of conduct would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art where there is a design need or market pressure to solve a problem and there are a finite number of identified, predictable solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR allows taking account of inferences and creative steps that a skilled artisan would employ. If the known options are finite and predictable and pursuing them would likely lead to success, 'obvious to try' can show obviousness (KSR 550 U.S. at 421). The converse: §103 bars patents for predictable uses of prior art elements unless the improvement is more than predictable use (see In re Kubin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness need not seek precise teachings; can rely on inferences/creative steps
rubrics_metrics.description: An obviousness analysis need not seek out precise teachings directed to the specific subject matter of the challenged claim, because a court can take account of the inferences and creative steps that a person of ordinary skill would employ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR indicates that a skilled artisan's ability to combine, infer, or adapt teachings can support an obviousness determination even when the prior art does not spell out the exact claimed subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation requires every claim element in a single reference
rubrics_metrics.description: For a claim to be anticipated, each claim element must be disclosed, either expressly or inherently, in a single prior art reference, and the claimed arrangement or combination of those elements must also be disclosed, either expressly or inherently, in that same reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Therasense; Sanofi-Synthelabo. Anticipation is a strict test: every limitation must be found in the four corners of one reference (or inherently).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency standard for anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference may anticipate inherently if a claim limitation that is not expressly disclosed is necessarily present, or inherent, in the single anticipating reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'very essence of inherency' is that one of ordinary skill would recognize the reference unavoidably teaches the property. Possibility or likelihood is insufficient—there must be necessity (see Verizon; Agilent). The Board applied this when finding NCT ’653 did not inherently disclose a device that necessarily 'contains and delivers' a 162 mg fixed dose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preponderance of the evidence burden in IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner in an IPR must show unpatentability (anticipation or obviousness) by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board evaluates prior art and arguments under the preponderance standard; failure to carry this burden results in denial of the ground (applied in analysis of NCT ’653 relative to claims 1 and 5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for prior art to cure deficiencies in another reference when combining
rubrics_metrics.description: When asserting obviousness over a combination of references, each reference should supply teaching that cures deficiencies in the others such that their combination would have been motivated and carried out with reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board examines whether one reference teaches how to make or use what the other lacks (e.g., formulation vs delivery device) and whether the combined teachings would have been routine or would have required undue experimentation. Teaching away, or lack of enabling disclosure for a required feature, undermines the proposed combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of public accessibility for documentary/prior art evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: To rely on a public document (e.g., a ClinicalTrials.gov record) as a prior art reference, the petitioner must prove the document was publicly accessible before the priority date, typically via reliable evidence and an adequate declarant showing how the document would have been found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declarations proving public accessibility should identify search methods and be from a qualified declarant or otherwise establish that a person of ordinary skill would have located the record. Vague attestations or search-by-identifier only (rather than realistic prior-art search strategies) may be insufficient. The Board scrutinized the Lassman declaration for such deficiencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away and risk considerations in motivation analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that prior art teaches away from a proposed combination, or shows technical risk (e.g., concerns about concentration, volume, immunogenicity), weighs against a finding of motivation to combine and reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board considers contemporaneous technical concerns (solubility/concentration limits, injection volume limits, immunogenicity risks) and whether the art advised dividing doses or otherwise discouraged the single-device solution. Patent Owner's technical evidence that high-concentration/large-volume SC dosing was challenging was used to argue against obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations that require specific device disclosure cannot be supplied by mere implication
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite a specific functional device (e.g., 'a subcutaneous administration device, which contains and delivers to a patient a 162 mg fixed dose') require disclosure in the prior art that the device both exists and necessarily performs that function; mere mention of subcutaneous administration without device disclosure may be insufficient for anticipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board analyzed whether NCT ’653's statement that patients receive drug subcutaneously inherently disclosed a device that contains and delivers the entire fixed dose; because multiple-injection possibilities were not excluded, inherency failed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence supporting reasonable expectation: routine predictive techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner may rely on routine predictive techniques (e.g., pharmacokinetic modeling) and available prior-art parameters (or reasonable estimates thereof) to show a reasonable expectation that a proposed dosing regimen would work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert testimony that routine two-compartment PK modeling (using prior-art parameters or reasonable estimates) would predict therapeutic concentrations can support a reasonable expectation of success, provided the modeling and parameter assumptions are justified and not speculative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid importing unclaimed limitations (no disease if not claimed)
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not improperly import into claims limitations (such as a particular disease) that are not recited; claims that do not recite efficacy or a disease generally should not be limited by such unrecited features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioner argued it was improper to read a disease limitation into claims that do not recite a disease (citing Acceleration Bay), which affects whether efficacy is a required limitation for the obviousness analysis.
